blocks.x: Okay, well we're interviewing Joe Watkins this March 24th, 1969. Just going from what you're about to say, Joe, about when you started music.

When I started, I started in 1920s. Well that was quite a few years after George Lewis and Paul Barbrain. Well I always did love drums because I was born in the third ward and that was, a section for jazz probably because Lee Armstrong was from that ward. He was born and raised around there. And I don't know about Joe Oliver because I always heard that Joe was not exactly from the Orlins. But it was him, Lee Armstrong, Funk Johnson, and you had Manuel Moneta. And, uh, was this other fella's name, uh, was a good trumpet man. His name started when it was Kimball. Oh, I can't think of the other ones in here. But anyhow, most of your leaders came from out of that ward. Well I've taken, I've taken a liking to drums. Well we had Henry Morton in them days, Baber Dodds, Zutty Singleton. And, uh, well I had other little few drummers like a fella called Two Bits, Sun Shop, or Cook Shop Sun. And, uh, well I used to go listen to most of the Baber Dodds. But at later years, when I did try to start around the 1920s, I was taking fresh roll lessons from Henry Morton. And, uh, on a board with a piece of round drum skin, oh I'd say about eight inches in diameter. And he used to learn me how to roll right in the center of that piece of skin. Well I had bought me a drum, a snare drum, and then they had them light, uh, drums, and they didn't have the metal drums like we have today. Well, I took several lessons from him. And, uh, a while after that I gave it up. Then I met Paul Barbrand. Well, he was gonna learn me how to read music, but after he asked me what I wanted to play, I said, I want to play jazz drums. He said, well, you don't particularly need to learn the four sheets. He said, all you got to learn is your fresh roll, learn how to count your time, and so on. Well, he used to come by the house I was living down on, right here on Lafitte between Galveston, not Galveston, between, uh, Durbany and, uh, Claiborne. Well, he used to come there several times and give me a few lessons, learn me how to read the notes. But after that he said, well, you don't particularly, particularly need that if, whenever you're ready, you want to start. He said, well, you got the idea of the tempo. Well, I didn't have no drums then. So, in 1928, no, 21, I sent off to a woodless factory and bought me a set. Well, in them times they had the overhanging pedal. Foot pedal for the bass drum, side cymbal, a little small Chinese tum tum, about ten inches in diameter, and an old Chinese crash cymbal. They then used a zillion cymbals in them days like they're using them now. And, uh, and I used, uh, well, we had them move, I had them move down to, uh, Johnson near Lafitte. And I used to set up my drums in the daytime and I have one of them old Ten Cents Kazoots, that you put in your mouth and hum the songs through it. Well, I started practicing that-a-way until I got the tempo straight. Well, at that time I was working as a night porter at the Whitney National Bank for Main Office, St. Charles and Grabby. Well, that's where I met Eddie Dawson. He was a porter night janitor over there. And there was another fellow who was working there by the name of Bud Russel, a bass player. Well, we all got friendly together, you know, and they found out that I was trying to come up in the music world. Well, most of their work used to be in the Irish Channel. They used to get a lot of work out there for white and colored. So I played out there with them and, uh, a fella called Dude and his brother. Well, I was, uh, they played mostly blues, like very few up tempos that they played mostly, all moderate, like, you know, moderate tempo. Well, I continued to play with them until 1928. And, uh, well, I gave it up in 1928 because business had got kind of bad then. I said, there's no need to continue now, I said, because there ain't nothing to it. So I stopped playing up until 19...1935. And I met Walter Nelson, a steel guitar player. He's got old Pico's place down at, uh, Oysalon and Robinson. One day we were sitting down, we met, went up by some friends of ours up on the Biemble Street. And, well, the fella that lived there with his family, he was a drummer too. So Walter noticed when I was patting my foot in the temple with his guitar playing, he asked me, he said, you play drum? I said, I used to. He said, you can get back in the business. I said, there ain't nothing in it these days. I said, because it looks like it's just been dropped out of sight. He said, once you try to get your second hand set and start back, he said, I can get some work for you. So sure enough, I've done it and he started getting me work. Well, at that time...
What sort of date was this? Huh? What date was this about?

Oh, that was around in the 1940s. Yeah, in the 1940s, because I was living across the street at the time, at 825 North Galvestre. And the first job that, after he found out that I was playing that good, Herbert Moran, one of our old time trumpet men, he was a wonderful jazz man on the trumpet. He left Chicago and came back home. And he heard me play. He said, Joe, he said, why don't you try to stick with the drums? I said, well, if I'm playing that good, I said, I don't mind sticking with it, but if I'm bad, I said, I'd much rather get out of it. So, the first job we got together was the three of us. It was him, Walter Nelson on the guitar, and myself on the drums. We played a job back in Gentilly, in a barn, a cow barn, a stall, you know. Okay, I was in one stall, he was in the other two stalls. Now, we had, now I had trouble trying to listen to what the heck they was playing, see. But, the acoustic in that place must have been mildly good, because the sound was coming over fine. Well, after that, Walter Nelson had got a job at the Silver Star nightclub at St. Pernod and St. Claude on the downtown in River Corner. It was run by Joe Cianelli. Well, we started playing there every Friday and Saturday. Well, we used to have a little difficulty in hiring musicians outside of Moraine and myself. We'd cut the job call for six men. Well, we used to hire George Lewis, we used to hire Slowdray. And we had a fellow on saxophone from uptown by the name of Albert. I never did know his full name, but I knew they called him Albert, but he was a darn good sax man. Well, we used to play there every weekend until one Saturday night he put in a flow show. Well, he didn't have no license for that. So, the Lord stepped in and took us all down. So, I had to pay a ten dollar fine. My wife paid a ten dollar fine to get me out. Well, I said, never no more of Joe Cianelli's Silver Star for me, if that's the way he's going to operate. So, in the meantime, we were bringing our jobs around town. George Lewis had got a job to play on that voidsman for a prizefighter back at the Pelican ballpark. So, when we got through playing at that voidsman, he said, Joe, he said, how about joining up with me? Well, that was after he had come back from New York. That was in 1945. I said, yeah, I said, I'll play with you until somebody better comes along. He said, all right, he said, you can play all jobs with me. Well, we started getting jobs out in the, uh, one of them Catholic schools out in town there. I forget the name of the school, but I can't think of it right now, anyhow. But anyway, I continued to play with him, and he told me, he said, Joe, I like the way you're playing. You're playing that old style drumming and that's what I want. He said, I'm going to keep this thing going. He said, now we done revived it in New York, and we're going to try to keep it going here. He said, it'll take a little time to build up, but he said, it'll come through. Well, sure enough, it did come through. We played at the Royal Room on Royal Street one night, or whatever, during the time of Tony Almericka's reign. He was, he used to play there all the time.
Yes. Would that be the Parisian Room?

The Parisian Room, yeah. Yeah, the Parisian Room. Well, we played there one Saturday night, and the Almerocka Club had warned us. So, after we got through playing there was this fellow, Eddie Kidd Wolf, former friend, a dry spider, and his partner was named Frank. He was an Italian. Well, when we got through playing at the Parisian Room, we went there and finished out the night, because we knocked off at 12 o'clock at the Parisian Room. And we went there and played a couple hours until 2 o'clock in the morning. Well, they hired us to play every night. Well, we played there for over a year. And that's where this big blow-up of this band got recognition in the Look magazine. I guess you remember that. Well, we started traveling, and at that time when we was playing there, Reverend Kershaw and his wife and Professor Ball of the University of Cincinnati was down here for a band. Well, they started from Myrtleville in Boivin, where we was playing there, Almerocka, and went down in every place that had a band. And they selected us. Well, when we went to Cincinnati, we made a tape for the archives of the University of Cincinnati. Well, after we made that tape, we played a concert for the University of Cincinnati. And we left there and went into Oxford, Ohio. And after that, they started bringing us out there regularly. We started going into Bloomington. We went into Bloomington, Indiana. We went to, uh, oh. Well, anyway, we covered a lot of territory in Ohio. Then we started traveling to California. We started alternating in California between, uh, Los Angeles and San Francisco. See? We played three months at the Beverly Cavern, and played three months for Doc at the Hangover in San Francisco. Doc, who? All I knew was Doc. That's what we used to call him, you know, Doc. Well, anyhow, after we wound up there, we went to start working at the Tin Angel. That was on Embarcadera. Embarcadera, and, oh, I can't think of the name. It's simple, too. But anyhow, we started working there every night. That was around 50, or the part of 57. Well, at that time they wanted George Lewis band in England, but he had to make an appearance face over there. Well, he left the band in my charge, and mistake taking him over to England.
That was in 57.

Yeah, that was in 57. Well, he made several, uh, he made a tour of England. And, uh, when he came back, we were still in Frisco. We made a recording. I think it was Empirical. It's a red record. You may have that record.
The Empirical record was the one made in Ohio.
That was the one made in Ohio. Well, we made a red record on Powell Street in San Francisco. I can't think of the name of that company. We had Tom Jefferson on trumpet.
Is it Cavalier?

I think it was Cavalier. Yeah, I'm more than sure it was Cavalier. Because we had Tom Jefferson on trumpet at that time. Well, anyway, after we got through playing in Frisco, where we came on back home, where Elton, he stopped off in Los Angeles, so he was going to make up his mind to stay there. Well, sure enough, he did. So we came on back home, and we started to play a little odd jobs around town, you know, until something else was popped. So sure enough, came the word from England that they wanted to ban over there. Well, we went over there. We left on the 28th of December, 1958. And we arrived in London, in Liverpool, in early January of 1959. I think it was around the 6th or the 7th or something like that. But anyway, we got there before the 10th of January. Well, we stayed overnight in Liverpool, then we went on up to London. Got trained. We got to London. Ken Collier had his brass band out at the station, the Union Station. They had one over there, you know. And they was playing so much like New Orleans. I said, now I wanted Poison and them to beat us over here and got the band lined up, because I couldn't see for the crowd, you know. Well, as we was marching up to the front, I found out it was Ken Collier's brass band. And they was playing just a little while to stay here. I said, that sounds so much like Poison's brass band. And it was them. Well, Barry, he was on drums. Well, I hadn't met none of them fellas yet, but I hadn't met Ken Collier when he toured over here with us. So we went on to a hotel. I was so nervous. When we got to the hotel, they saw I was shaking. So Jimmy Ashman said, you want a hot cup of tea? He said, quads your nerves. I said, I'd have to have something. Because they wasn't serving the guy that out. So I said, I got to have something, Jimmy. I said, so he gave me a hot cup of tea. And I got all right. Well, we stopped at that hotel, the Empirical Hotel. Well, we stopped there for a little time. Well, in fact, it was a whole week before we did go to work. It gave us a lot of time to get around and view the sights and meet a lot of the people and everything, you know. So, we played, we came back, the first job was to play in Liverpool. And after we left Liverpool, then we started going to Manchester, Birmingham, Brighton, and all them different places playing concerts. Well, we played there, I think, around there for about a month. After we left there, we went to Sweden. No, Denmark. Went to Denmark. We played a concert there. We stayed there for about a week. We left from there. We went to Sweden. What do you call it? Stockholm, Sweden. We played a concert over there in a big gymnasium. And they had a wonderful crowd that turned out. And we was greeted wonderfully by the people. Before we had a chance to start playing, we was on a march to the place. And they wanted to know if we was coming back. I said, yeah, we'll be back. You know, make them feel good. Well, it snowed so much in Sweden, we didn't have a chance to get out to see anything. I mean, it snowed all. When we got there, it snowed and we left, it was snowing. So, I had boys that wanted something to drink. I said, well, I'll go get it. I said, how close is the place? I said, right around the corner. So, when I walked outside, man, ice looked like it was about that thick on the sidewalk. So, I kind of skidded around the corner and got us a bottle. And we all stayed up in the hotel and had two newspaper girl reporters came by and wanted to interview us. And so, we all sat down and drank. So, they forgot the interviews. So, they went on home, you see. And then, we came back to Sweden. Well, anyway, we came back to Denmark.
Sweden.
Yeah, that's Sweden. Yeah, that's right. That was in Sweden.
Yeah, then you went back to Denmark.

Then we went back to Denmark and we left from there and went to Baden-Baden, Germany for a week for a TV show. So, naturally, it was more of a cabaret scene. And we rehearsed that whole week. And when we finished there, we left and went back to London. And that was when, well, everything was over with. Then the boys got ready to come on. Well, Joe Rovershow, Howard, Jim, Miss Tate, George, they all left by plane. Well, Jack and I came back by boat. And that was when we run into that 80-mile gale. And I'm telling you, it was really rough. Well, when we landed in New York, it had been snowing there, too. And that's where I started to feel my pains. So, we came on back home. Then they walked us back in Ohio again, in Cincinnati. Well, at the Sinton Hotel. The Sinton, S-I-N-T-O-N, Sinton Hotel. Well, we went to work there for a couple of months, I believe. Well, we stayed in the hotel right where we was playing. So, we got through there. We came on back to New Orleans. And the Sheraton Gibson warned us. Well, we went on back there. What was that? That was right around the corner from where the Sinton was on, uh...
In Cincinnati, something?

On 6th Street or 5th Street. That was in Cincinnati. Uh, we played there about six weeks or eight weeks. That was a whole band? Yeah, that was a whole band. We had, uh... We had on trumpet. Howard. Yes, Howard was on trumpet. And then we had, uh, this is a crippled trombone player there. Because Jim had taken the sick and they got him to work in his place. Oh, he plays with... He was playing with Bob Bob, Brandon, all the time.
Oh, I know what you mean by Derek, or Bob, Frog.

Frog, yeah. Well, he played with us. And, uh... And at that time, Dregg happened to be sick. We had, uh, Adams, Classy Adams, on bass. So after that, we, uh, came on back home and... That's where George had taken sick. Wasn't feeling any too well. He said he was feeling too bad to travel too much. On them strenuous trips like that, you know? Well, anyway... That's when Larry... That's when Larry... Started this, uh, jazz thing off. But he was having, uh... Just piano playing... Until he ran into punch. I had this place next door to the preservation hall. So I was told. But I went out there one day.
Now, you were sick yourself around about this time, weren't you?

Yeah, I was. Yeah, I was sick. But not, you know, like I am now, you know? I was getting around, but it was pretty tough. But anyway... I'll give Larry credit... For starting off this jazz revival. Not, uh, not starting it off, but keeping it going. Because he took in, uh, I don't know what this place, what the hall was before he... Put the bands in there. But they tell me that punch... With the voice band to start working in there. Mm-hmm. And then he start rounding up the other old musicians and... And giving them a break, you know, and bringing them in. So that's how they come to have, uh... And then he came back for, uh, this former leader of the, uh... Creole... Oh, it's a bright fella that played trumpet from downtown. His name was Pete. Creole Serenators. Mm-hmm. Well, he had a band, didn't he? He had a band in there. Wendell Eugene.
Yeah, Wendell Eugene, yeah.

Wendell Eugene plays, uh, slide. Well, he played a couple of times in there, because I had hired him. When, uh, Jim couldn't make it, so I would get him, you know. So... Well, he said he couldn't keep it up, he said, because he was walking too much in the daytime to live in the mail. So, uh... After him, Jim came back. And he started playing again. And they put Poise in there with his band. That was with Emma. And who else did they have? I think she had a band in that, that one, at the early times.
Well, that was the time when you were playing there on weekends with what they call the All-Star Band. Do you remember?

Yeah. And George, yeah. That's right. Yeah, that was the All-Stars that played then. And, uh... Well, first thing, next thing came up was Japan. Yes. Jeff asked him, said, Joe, you'd like to go to Japan? I said, yeah, what is Spain? He told me.
That was 63.

That was 1963, up in office, I believe. I told him, yeah. I said, who with? He said, well, Joe Band, George. I said, well, all right. Well, Jim didn't want to go. So you got Nelson, George, Papa John Joseph, Robichaud piano, I was on drums, and Punch. And we all agreed to go. He said, there was a three-month tour. I said, yeah, I don't mind it. Well, we went over there, and we really made a smashing hit with the people. They really went for jazz, like hook, line, and sinker. They loved it. And we stayed over there for them three months. And we went back to Tokyo. Well, we came back to Tokyo the day that the president was assassinated. I think we were stopping at the Prince Hotel. And they had the news in the paper, you know, over there in American, you know, so you could read it. Well, they claimed two holidays for the whole of Japan, which I thought was very nice of them, very respectable of them. And we left the following day, and we went back to Honolulu. We didn't play. We stayed there for a couple of days. And we left by plane and came back to New Orleans on the 3rd of December 1963. And I've been home ever since.
That was the last tour you went on?
That was the last tour I went on. So...
You didn't go on any other trips to Japan? No.

No, I didn't go on no other trip at the time, because I called George and told him, I said, George, I think you're going to have to get another drummer, because my wife is very sick, and there's nobody but me to look after. So I'm going to have to call it off. I said, I'll play at the hall. I said, I'm freelancing. I said, I'll play with anybody that hires me. But I said, when they come down to making a trip anyway, I don't care if it's the Baton Rouge, Bugger Lou Sunday, I don't want to go out of town at the present time. That's why my wife is sick like she is. Well, he told me, all right, he wasn't angry or nothing about us, you know. Well, anyway, I stayed here and I looked after the best way I could, and I was still playing out there at the hall. Well, it had gotten so I had to put in the hospital. That was during the year of 1966, around Easter time. I put in there on a Friday before Palm Sunday, and she stayed in there until Good Friday. So Good Friday night, they brought her back in the ambulance. And I started taking care of her just the same as I was doing before. And all the neighbors there was getting kind of uneasy. I said, Mr. Joe, I said, you're beginning to look kind of very broke down running so much. I said, who else going to do it for me? I can't afford to pay nobody to run my errands. So naturally, I'll have to do them myself. So, on the 26th of June 1966, she died. 1966.

We buried on the 27th of June 1966. And it was during that time before she died that I started to take the seat. My legs had went bad on me. I used to have to use a chair to slide around on. You know, taking foot in this slide wherever I had to go to the bathroom. I had to slide in with the chair pulling along with me. So, I had gotten sold a week back then. Yeah, I was in the hospital about six weeks. I came out after July 4th. Must have been about a week after the 4th of July. Came home. I still couldn't do nothing for her. But I tried to get around the best way I could. But it looked like it was the hardest thing in the world for me to get enough appetite to eat. So, I called Jabber and I told him about it. He said, well, see the best thing for you to do is to go to a rest home. Maybe you need rest. I said, yeah, probably. So, I said, because I can't eat. I don't have an appetite. So, he said, well, we're going to take you to the rest home. So, sure enough, he came down the next morning early. He got me at them. Made arrangements for them up at the Hubbard home up in Carlton on Hamilton Street. And they brought me there. Well, that day they were serving oxtail stew. Well, I really enjoyed it. And they had greens with it. Well, his wife was with us and she told me, she said, Joe, now you eat all the greens you can. I said, I will. If that's going to help me, I'm going to do that. Well, I went in there on the last, the second, the last day of September of 1966. But I got so disgusted with the place. It was supposed to be somebody there that helped me to learn how to walk again. I didn't get that accommodation. I said, well, I can't stay here. I'm paying all this money. And all I'm getting is just three meals of there and they ain't worth a penny. I do better at home myself. So sure enough, I just got disgusted and left on the 15th of December of 1966. That was before my wife died. I came on home. I said, I got, I just, she wanted to find out. She asked me all kinds of questions. I said, I just want to go home. I said, I'm feeling better. I said, I just want to go home. So they released me. She got kind of angry. She said, well, you cannot get back in here no more. I said, I don't want to come back. I said, I'd much rather stay home and die if I can't do no better. So sure enough, a friend of mine, cab driver Pickle, came and got me, helped to bring me upstairs. And that's where I've been ever since. Outside the time I go out to the hall at, to the jam section. Cause I ain't been able to go out nowhere to buy no groceries or go shopping or nothing like that yet. Because my left leg is still kind of wobbly yet, you know.
Do you have any plans for, do you foresee that you will be going on any more tours?

Well, I'm expecting a tour next year. That's why I say I want to take my time and build myself up strong like I want to be. Cause Barry Martin is working up a deal for me to make a tour with his band. Cause a lot of my friends over there in England and in Italy and Brussels, people I've never seen. But they've all heard of me and they've heard my records, heard the records of me. They all would like for him to make some kind of arrangement. That he could bring me over there. And that's what he's been writing to me about where he'll be down here in June.
Is he coming here?
Yeah, he's supposed to be on that jazz fest. Oh.
You see.

And if I can make it, I'll try to be on it. Is Simon Richardson coming here? I don't know. Because I haven't received one letter from Sammy Remington. Since he went back to England, but I heard he moved to Denmark. Yeah.
Tell me.
I think that was the last letter I got from him. Or somebody wrote and told me that they saw him in Denmark.
When you were on this tour in Europe in 59, didn't Sammy go with you and play you for a bit on that?
Not with me.
I thought you said, no, maybe you... No, not with the George Lewis group. I'm thinking of a different time, I think. I think there was a time...
Because we didn't even have a banjo player. Oh. No. Only six of us went over at first time in 59. Right.
Let me ask you about playing with the George Lewis band and what sort of a band you thought it was and how you played and how you particularly yourself played.

Well, I'll tell you, Tom. George Lewis wanted the best or nothing at all. And he did get that recognition for his rhythm section. He was supposed to have the best rhythm section on it. That was including Elton Pennell, Slow Drag, Lawrence, and myself. And when he got that, he was satisfied. But, he wants you to keep that drive. See, that was a driving beat that he had me working on. That wasn't exactly what you would call an authentic jazz beat. See? Because if you listen plainly to Saeed, you don't hear that beat. And neither was Paul doing it. No. Ain't none of them fellas want to do that beat.
Did George give you any particular instructions as to how he wanted you to play?
That was all he wanted me to do was just give him that drive beat. That was all he wanted. Just keep the band going.
Did he say anything about anything like bass drum or cymbals or anything like that?
Cymbals. It was cymbals all the time. Start to finish.
Did he say he wanted that?

Yeah. He wanted to start off on a cymbal and finish up on a cymbal like a swing band. See, I used to get angry, but I said, well, what can I do? He's the leader. He knows what he wants. But the balance of the fellas in the band would get angry with me. I said, it's not my fault. I said, y'all speak to the leader about it. I'm not playing the way I want to play. If I'm playing the way I want to play, I'll be playing the old style way. The way I'm supposed to play if I'm going to play authentic jazz. But I said, he wants to drive beats so naturally I have to give it to him. See? I said, other than that, I said, it's just after y'all with him. Because Jim used to get on me, Howard would get on me. Another time they'd get on drag, but he was beaten too fast and all that. I said, what? Point to George. He's the one that wants to drive so we got to give it to him.
Let me ask you about some of the earlier episodes again. Do you remember playing at Manny's? Manny's Tavern.

Manny's Tavern. Benefit and Sing Rock. Tell me about that. Yeah, well we played back there every weekend. On Friday nights, Saturday nights, no Sundays. We played back there every weekend. Oh, I can't say how long we played back there. We stayed there for quite a while before we went on Boyfriend Street. See, that was when we first went back there, it was Manny's.
What sort of a place was it?
Nice place. Very nice. Never had no trouble back there at all. Dancing?
Yeah.

Because we was playing back in the dance hall. You see, the bar was up in the front. And the dance hall was in the back. Big dance hall. So there was a lot of tourists that used to come back there, you know, and listen to us. Pete Fountain used to come there before he started. And Frank Asunder and his brother, Freddie, they used to come and sit in with us. And this young trumpet player there, George, I can't think of his last name. But he was a wonderful trumpet man. He used to play with the bass of Street Six. He was playing that, what you call it, that, Fuebren and Conti. Well, he used to work that one time every night until he died.
Yes, I know he was a trumpet player.
Yeah, his name was George. He was an Italian fellow, too. Well, yeah, we played at Manley's a long time before we got to a real break.
What about, where else on Burden did you play apart from...

Well, now, let me see now. I think we played a little short time at the Silver Slipper. Yeah, at that time we had Nick Gaglianna as our manager. We got us a job there and we stayed there for a while. Then they brought in a band from England and they got rid of them, I think, in a week's time because they didn't like the way they was dressing with that long hair and all that. So they soon got rid of them and we played at the Mardi Gras Lounge, Sydney. We played there for quite a while. And we played at the Paddock Lounge.
What was it like playing on Burden Street?

Well, it was all right. Nobody worried us. They hardly requested any numbers. They left us playing what we wanted to play. Outside of the Paddock Lounge, you got Miss Valenti. She didn't want you to play nothing slow. And that's what got George upset. He said, I'm going to play some slow numbers because I ain't going to be a racehorse in those numbers after every number we play. He said, I'm going to mix them up. But she didn't say nothing about it. So we stayed there for, oh, for a long time. A little less than a year though.
Is it harder work playing on Burden Street than anywhere else?

In some of them places, the hours is too long. You go to work at 8.30 and knock off around 3 o'clock in the morning. Now on a Saturday night, you don't know what time you're going to get off. You knock off around 3.30, maybe 4 o'clock in the morning, according to the crowd they have. If you've got a good crowd, they want the band to stay there. See?
Where are all the places you've played all over the world? Where did you enjoy most?

Well, I'm going to tell you the truth, Tom. I enjoyed them all. I really did enjoy them all. I don't think one I did the other. But everywhere we went, we were treated royally. Nobody scorned us because we were what we are. Nobody overlooked us or nothing. They really enjoyed our playing. They enjoyed our company. And that was one thing that made me happy and actually that made us play better. Because we were treated like human beings. But you take like down and, well, I don't want to say it. You're scared the whole time you're in there. So I just, we just played a couple of jobs down there when that was all. After we heard about what they had done to Papa Celestan's band, we didn't want to play down there anymore. We took all the instruments and dumped them in the bar or something down there. We don't care to play for them kind of people. But now they got no more civilized. I don't know if any bands go down there now. I never hear of any of them.
Where is that?
Down in, what's that island where they do all that fishing? Grand Isles and all around them places down there. Oh, yeah.
Do you think the situation has changed with regard to the...

Oh, I'm more than sure it's changed. Yeah, I'm more than sure it's changed because you don't hear of any, any difficulty in the people getting along down there these days. At one time it used to be, poor black men had to be scared to poke his head out the door almost. But I think now it's 100% better. Since they've started this integration now they all coming to the common sense and trying to get... See I think jazz, I mean authentic jazz, I think it has done more. More towards developing integration than president or anybody ever brought together. Because you notice yourself how they mixing up out there at the hall. Because I was surprised to see the colored people going out there like they do now, you know. And getting in them hotels and all that. And I always say I think it's this jazz music because... Where for a brass band is playing you could see almost as many white people out there as they got color. It's just bringing them together in a nice way. That's the way I look at it, you know. And all I've got to say is... All these old time jazz musicians... Treat them people nice. Because they are the ones, to my knowledge, that's got this thing on top. What I mean is them that brought it to the front for everybody to see that it's a decent music. Like see now the kid coming up to use a call of the bad type of music. And they would even spell it wrong. See. Well now the kid is going to call it J-A-S-S. But now it's J-A-Z-Z. See. Well I think that's the most appropriate number for unemployed.
What do you think of the future of music?

Well... To tell you the truth, Tom... My people is going to rock and roll the youngsters. Look like they prefer that. Now there's some youngsters that like jazz. Because I can tell from those that I see out there at the hall. There's a lot of them come out there. But I think that jazz is the unfilled its foundation to stay. But there can always be some old musicians, some old jazz musicians around to play it.
What about in different parts of the world?
When I think over...
Covering the world, to tell you the truth about it...

Jazz is over there to stay. On the other side. But they're taking more of the jazz than anything else. Everywhere we went over there there was a jazz group. And now you take these college... American college boys. Every college you go to... Has got a little jazz group. All of them. The reason why I know that... Because everyone that we played a concert... They invited us out to a little gathering they had... And they had their little jazz groups to entertain us. And they're trying to play authentic jazz. See? But what they want to... What the most important thing they're trying to get together is the beat. That's what they want is the beat. That's what they want is the beat. And that's what I've been trying to teach them many of them. Because they'd all come and say, How you do this, how you do that, how you do the other. And I would take time during intermission and show them. See? Now I met a fellow one night in... Indianapolis. Youngster. Was playing with a 14-piece orchestra. When I was... And I was backstage. And Gary Nash and Simmons said, He said, How do you make a press roll? I said, Who you playing with? He said, I'm playing with... This 14-piece outfit. And I said to myself, He's playing with a 14-piece outfit And I don't know how to make a press roll. I found it strange. You know? I see a press roll is easy.
But a lot of them can't do it. I don't care who they are.

That goes for... What's this white drummer's name there? Caught with Dope. Oh... You can know him if I could call his name. Uh-huh. Gene Krupa? Yeah, Gene Krupa. You take this fellow Rich. All them fellas, they do all that stuff. They don't forgot how you make a press roll. You know what I mean? The press roll is just going out of their mind. All they want to do is just work on that stuff in front of them. Now you don't call them jazz drummers. They don't think how they make a press roll. No. They don't think how they make a press roll. See? Because all they want to do is just a solo. George told me one day, he said, Joe, you see all that you doing there on taking a solo? He said, you cut it out. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. He said, you cut it out. He said, it's alright to make an explosion because some of the numbers call for it. But he said, you try to stay off all that fancy stuff. He said, I'm going to tell you why. You're going to throw the band off. You're going to either increase or you're going to fall. And he didn't lie. But I listened to many of them drummers on TV taking solos and bands who hardly know where they exactly come in. Unless somebody just concentrating hard on how the numbers going, you understand, when they're supposed to come in and they're following behind him. So I just made up my mind to give it up. I said, he's
a little bit. What did you think of George as a clarinet player?
I think George was wonderful. He reminded me so much of Johnny Dodds. That was another top clarinetist we had. George reminded me so much of him.
What was it about George's playing that you liked?
George was a big fan. I mean, I liked the way he used to back me up on just a closer walk with him. He used to get in that low register and I just loved that.
What was it about his style that you liked?

George was a big fan. Well, I think it's a style he created himself. Now, I don't say it's the same style as Johnny Dodds, but I think it's a style that he created himself. And it's two boys that I know, I think that's got that same touch, just by listening to his recordings. That's Thomas Anton and Ian Wheeler of England. But they got his Burgundy Street down, Burgundy
Blue's Pat. What did you think of George's tone?

It's time. Tone. Tone. I like it. I like it better than the others. I don't know why, but it's, I don't know, there's a sound that comes out there, you know, I don't know, it looks like it just gets to you. And I just enjoyed it. And I just loved to sit behind him when he was living, we was playing together. Because he really had a tune on that, I forgot what was the make of it, or BAM system or something like that. But anyhow, I just loved the way he played it. And I liked the way that Lawrence played his banjo. He wasn't a fancy man on picking numbers, but he kept that straight time. He was a good timekeeper. I never heard him, of course, but I just heard him. Yeah, he was a wonderful timekeeper.
Yes, indeed. Do you remember when you made those records for Souchon? Yeah, at Bedita and Verone. Tell me about that, what you can remember about that.

Well, I don't remember much about that. I know there was Elmer Talbot on trumpet, Slowdrek on bass, George. You don't remember the circumstances? I don't think we had any piano. And we had a song banjo. I think it was six of us. Well, we played up on the second floor. Right up over that music, they had a music store then, downstairs on the first floor. And we played upstairs on the second floor. And we, I think we stopped around about eight o'clock. And we didn't wind up till two o'clock the next morning. So we just played back, played back, played back. You know. Very fine record then. Yeah. And you know I haven't heard it since we made it. You haven't?
Got a wonderful beat. There's something about the beat that's another you wanted to mention. Yeah. But that early period, 1950, it seemed like the beat was much better then than, I mean,
later then. Yeah, that's right. You were talking about the beat change. Mm-hmm. Well, that was George doing, changing everything. He didn't want this, he didn't want that. So, naturally.
It was partly Lawrence leaving the band too, I think. Lawrence is one of the ones that made the beat so good, I think.

Oh, yeah. Yeah, he did. Yeah, he had a lot to do with it. Because he didn't, uh, he didn't fall off at no time. The only time he got mad is when George would get me on them, on them racehorse tempos, then he would say something. Because he used to tell George all the time, he said, George, he said, what's the idea of having, keeping Joe on the cymbal from start to finish, he don't need no snare drum. See, I think the man should play the snare drum sometime.
Did George kick off the tempos? Always did.
Yeah. He always kicked it off, kicked off the tempos. Mm-hmm. And if you didn't come in right with him, he was gonna look back at you and make signs with his clam that'd come up.
Mm-hmm. Did you ever rehearse at any time, that band?
With the band? Yeah. Did that band rehearse?
When the voice started. What, how would you rehearse? Can you tell me about how the band rehearsed?

Well, there wasn't many rehearsals, because we, at that time, we had got kind of busy. One time we rehearsed in George Lewis' backyard. I don't know if it was down on Burgundy Street. They got the picture of it in the Look magazine. Mm-hmm. I've seen that.
You saw that. This last week they had that? Yeah. Did you get that? Did you get a copy of that?

Yeah, I had a copy of it. I don't know where the heck I put it. I got it there somewhere. Yeah, I got it there somewhere. Well, anyhow, we rehearsed there. And then we used to rehearse across the street at my house, where I was living at 825. We had more rehearsals there than we did anywhere else.
Did you ever rehearse with, using records?
No. No, except now listen to a record and try to play.
I heard that from someone that you did that on some of those tunes, maybe that you hadn't known too well, like, I can't think of the tune, Canal Street Blues or something like that.
No. I never heard that played on a recording, because we used to play that with Sidney DeVille when we was working at his club. Which one was that? The Mardi Gras.
The Billets and DeVille.

Yeah. Well, when we was working there, we used to play that a many times with him, but we never faded off a record. But that was his favorite number, you know, that was one of the numbers that made him famous, Canal Street Blues. But, I'll say this, the fellas is passing off, the New Year's starts off kind of rough, but it's slowing up a little bit, and I hope it stays slow for a long time. Because we have quite a few pioneers left. And I'm hoping that they don't fall by the wayside, like George and Drag and Paul and several other fellas ahead of them. But anyway, they did give the world this authentic jazz music, which I'm in hopes and praying that it will stay as long as possible. Never leave. Never leave. Because I find jazz is a music that moves people. I noticed just at the concert when I was sitting behind the drums. I was thinking about how the people that were sitting out in the audience, and them bands started blasting out there, man, they forgot they were sitting out. All you could see was everybody standing up clapping. Because, you see, the bands was alternating, the brass bands. See, the onward band and the Eureka brass band. I think the Eureka brass band made a circle three times. And then the onward brass band would make a circle three times. And then one thing, they would stop in front of the bandstand, and we would play along with them. See? Well, they played like that until it was time for the closing. You know, I think they closed around about 4.30 or something like that. Then we left, and, well, they invited me upstairs, so I went on upstairs and had a drink with them. Sit down there for a while. But I must say that it was a wonderful, I think it was a better concert than last year, because if it wouldn't, if the band would have been able to march from Canal and Nels Place, I don't think all that would have went on. Because it was the bad weather that made it like that, you know, and people really enjoyed themselves. Because I've done more singing, Emma, she's done more singing than we did last year. But last year she didn't sing close or walk with me, but this year she did.
So I think there's a couple, a few years left, right? Huh? I think there's a few years left yet for the music.

I think there's quite a few years. Yeah, it's quite a few years. But I, now if, if they may call, call it jazz. You know, jazz is not a music of arrangements. You know, you don't play arrangements in jazz. Because that ain't the way it starts, that's not the authentic type. But you take a lot of these bands now, they call themselves jazz band, but they make an arrangement for the clarinet player, the trumpet player, or the trombone player, or the drummer, you know, man. No, no, I just hate sockets, I may have been out here more than jazz like that. Jazz is a, is a gospel music, and it's a conversation music. If you come and say, Joe, I bought your friend, uh, that's a friend, or a Marsh Ratt Ramble, or something like that. All right, now you, you know how them numbers go. Now we strike up the band and play that number the authentic way, well that's just like talking to you. You understand what I mean? But if we gonna veer off to an arrangement, you say, well, they must be making a change. You see? But you don't make changes like that. Not in jazz. Jazz is an authenticated music. And I'm gonna play that way now, since George died, that's the way I'm gonna play. I'm gonna play the beat that's supposed to be played with that. I see, just like, Saeed was out there last week at the hall. He was telling, say, you know, a lot of these fellas go around here and talk about they're playing the jazz beat, but they're not. They said, jazz music is a single beat until you read it for the last two choruses to take out. Then you start to hitting that four, four beat with the cymbal. He said, now in between times, you feel like you wanna make a sound look better with the cymbal, all right. Pretty honest, simple, but likely.

segments.title: Opening and growing up in the Third Ward; drum lessons
segments.summary: Watkins describes the Third Ward jazz neighbourhood, early drummers he admired, and roll lessons from Henry Morton.

segments.title: First jobs: trio in a Gentilly barn and the Silver Star
segments.summary: Herbert Moran urges him to keep drumming; the trio with Walter Nelson plays a barn job, then the Silver Star nightclub with hired sidemen.

segments.title: Parisian Room, Almerocka and the Cincinnati and Ohio trips
segments.summary: The band plays the Parisian Room and Almerocka, gets Look magazine coverage, and is taken to Cincinnati, Ohio and Indiana; a record is made in Ohio and another in San Francisco.

segments.title: The 1959 England tour
segments.summary: They leave in December 1958 and reach Liverpool and London, meeting Ken Collier's brass band at the station; Sweden and Denmark follow.

segments.title: Return from Europe, Cincinnati hotel work and band members
segments.summary: After Germany and London the band returns, with a rough boat crossing, then works the Sinton Hotel in Cincinnati; he lists substitute players.

segments.title: Larry Borenstein's hall and the early Preservation Hall bands
segments.summary: Watkins credits Larry with keeping the jazz revival going by hiring the old musicians in his hall, and lists who played there.

segments.title: The 1963 Japan tour
segments.summary: Asked to go to Japan, he tours three months with Lewis's group, is in Tokyo the day the president is assassinated, and returns in December 1963.

segments.title: Giving up touring: his wife's death and his own illness
segments.summary: He stays home to nurse his sick wife, who dies in June 1966, then is hospitalised himself and goes to a rest home.

segments.title: Plans for a tour and clearing up the 1959 band lineup
segments.summary: He expects a tour with Barry Martin's band, asks after Sammy Rimington, and confirms six men went to Europe in 1959.

segments.title: Playing in the George Lewis band: the drive beat and cymbals
segments.summary: Lewis wanted a driving beat and cymbals start to finish; Watkins went along though it was not authentic and other members complained.

segments.title: Manny's Tavern on Bourbon Street
segments.summary: They played weekends in the back dance hall at Manny's, where tourists and young players like Pete Fountain sat in.

segments.title: Silver Slipper, Mardi Gras Lounge and the Paddock Lounge
segments.summary: Other Bourbon Street jobs, the owner's request for no slow numbers, and the long hours.

segments.title: Treatment around the world and segregation in Louisiana
segments.summary: He enjoyed everywhere, was treated well abroad, avoided fishing-island towns after what happened to Papa Celestin's band, and says jazz has helped integration.

segments.title: The future of jazz
segments.summary: Youngsters prefer rock and roll, but jazz will stay with the old musicians and spread abroad.

segments.title: Teaching the press roll and why George banned drum solos
segments.summary: Young drummers cannot make a press roll; Lewis told him to cut the fancy solos because they throw the band off.

segments.title: George Lewis as clarinetist, tone and Lawrence Marrero
segments.summary: He likens Lewis to Johnny Dodds, praises his low register and tone, and Lawrence Marrero's steady banjo timekeeping.

segments.title: Souchon recording session and the changing beat
segments.summary: He recalls a long record session over a music store, then discusses how the beat changed as Lewis changed things and Lawrence left.

segments.title: Rehearsals, Canal Street Blues and closing thoughts on jazz
segments.summary: The band rarely rehearsed, mostly at Lewis's yard or his house; he hopes the pioneers last and describes the brass bands at a concert.

segments.title: Jazz is not arrangements
segments.summary: Jazz is conversation music played the authentic way, not arrangements, and he will keep that beat now Lewis has died.
